source: Soloway, Bonar, Ehrlich (1983) Cognitive strategies and looping constructs: an empirical study (CACM 26(11)), read as a synopsis page
finding: People plan the loop in the order read-then-process, but standard Pascal while loops force process-then-read. When the language fit the preferred plan, more programs were correct.
numbers: 80% of written English plans used read/process. Correct programs: 52% in Pascal-L (exit-when loop) vs 33% in standard Pascal. Sample size not in the synopsis.
limits: Read a synopsis of the paper, not the paper. One 99999-average task. Experienced Pascal programmers shifted toward process/read, so the preferred plan depends on training.
agent_relevance: A plan written in the order the agent would naturally think is easier to turn into correct code than one forced into the host language's shape. Let the agent state the plan first, then map it.

source: Soloway, Bonar, Ehrlich (1983) Cognitive strategies and looping constructs: an empirical study (CACM 26(11)), read as a synopsis page
finding: Writing the English plan first and the program second showed that plan and code can disagree. The language that fit the plan raised correctness whichever strategy the person had chosen.
numbers: Hypothesis 2b (fit to the language-supported strategy raises correctness) was answered yes; hypothesis 3 (strategy varies with experience) was answered yes.
limits: Synopsis only; no test statistics or N reported there. One averaging task.
agent_relevance: Keep the plan and the code as two separate artifacts. Check that the code follows the plan, since mismatch is where errors enter.

source: Scholtz and Wiedenbeck (1992) An analysis of novice programmers learning a second language (PPIG 4)
finding: Novices who knew Pascal wrote a program in Pascal, Ada or Icon. Where the new language differed from Pascal in surface plan structure, they spent effort in predictable places (looking up constructs, rethinking control flow). Plan knowledge transferred only where structure matched.
numbers: Exploratory protocol study with tiny cells (the Pascal group had only three subjects; Ada and Icon about five each, read from a figure). Inter-rater agreement on coding planning episodes: 94.8%.
quote: ...a bottom up or plan creation methodology was more successful than a plan retrieval process.
limits: The PDF text is damaged by OCR in places; N per cell read from a figure. No inferential statistics. Exploratory by the authors' own description.
agent_relevance: Stored plans transfer when the target environment has the same structure. For a new tool or API, expect re-planning where structure differs, and put the checks there.

source: Scholtz and Wiedenbeck (1992) An analysis of novice programmers learning a second language (PPIG 4)
finding: When the target language was far from the known one, building the plan bottom up (start from the focal line, grow outward) worked better than recalling a whole plan top down. The find-A plan was retrieved forward more often than any other plan in all three languages.
numbers: Icon: 3 of 5 subjects built bottom up and all 3 produced working programs; the 2 who did neither forward nor mixed order did not. Pascal: 1 of 3 retrieved the complex loop plan forward. Ada: 1 of 5 forward.
limits: Very small N; the authors say the study raised more questions than it answered.
agent_relevance: Do not force top-down plan retrieval when the problem is unfamiliar. Offer a stored plan as a hint, but allow building from the core computation outward.

source: Scholtz and Wiedenbeck (1992) An analysis of novice programmers learning a second language (PPIG 4)
finding: Background cited in this paper: fewer than 60% of novices in first and second term courses finished any of three loop programs. The authors judge solutions that decompose data and then recompose it to be more error prone than solutions that operate on the whole structure.
numbers: Soloway cited: under 60% success on three looping programs. The second claim is the authors' own judgement.
limits: Secondary citation of Soloway; the second claim is not measured here.
agent_relevance: Composition of separately correct pieces is a weak point. Test the composed program, not only the parts.

source: Fisler (2014) The recurring rainfall problem (ICER 2014)
finding: Extension of Soloway's Rainfall plan-composition task to functional-first CS1. Students chose different high-level structures than in the imperative studies and made fewer low-level errors. Only 5% had no evident plan.
numbers: 218 student solutions across five courses at four schools (exam, lab or home; 10 to 30 minutes). Unclear structure: 31 of 218 (14%); no evident plan: 12 of 218 (5%). Six tasks required: sentinel, negative, sum, count, divide-by-zero, average.
limits: Input was a list, not keyboard I/O, so the problem differs from the original. One coder, no inter-coder reliability. Only a subset coded in some courses. Conditions differ across courses.
agent_relevance: The same task can be composed in several valid ways. Do not store one canonical plan; store the tasks and let the agent pick a composition.

source: Fisler (2014) The recurring rainfall problem (ICER 2014)
finding: Single traversal with interleaved tasks (the Soloway-style structure) was the minority choice. Cleaning the data first and then summing and counting was most common.
numbers: Of 187 solutions with a clear structure: Single Loop 38, Clean First 87, Clean Multiple 43 (the rest Clean After or No Cleaning).
limits: Course content drives this: two courses had not taught accumulator recursion. Fisler ties the choice to what students were taught.
agent_relevance: Plan choice follows what the agent has been shown. Examples in the prompt steer structure strongly.

source: Fisler (2014) The recurring rainfall problem (ICER 2014)
finding: Once students had a clear high-level structure, low-level error rates were low and between-task composition errors were rare. The classic claim that composing plans is the main source of bugs was not supported in this population.
numbers: Between-task composition error codes: 25 in the whole data set, only 3 in solutions with a clear structure. Zero-error share: Single Loop 74%, Clean First 66%, Clean Multiple 46%. 98 students had at least one non-missing error among 187 clear-structure solutions.
limits: Per-task coding can double count one source error. Single Loop vs Clean Multiple was not significant until one error type was removed (then p = .002). Single Loop students look like stronger programmers (confound).
agent_relevance: A clean decomposition with each task separate left few composition errors. Prefer separate small pieces over interleaved code.

source: Fisler (2014) The recurring rainfall problem (ICER 2014)
finding: Compared with older studies, these students did much better, and the gap stayed after dropping I/O. This points to teaching style, not the I/O plan alone, as a cause of the old failures.
numbers: Simon (149 students, C# CS1, input given in a structure): 36% had no pertinent code; Fisler: 3 to 6%. Simon: negatives ignored 40%, guarded division 0%. Ebrahimi's 20 LISP students: 50% missing if-guards, 40% misplaced updates, 40% malformed updates, 40% spurious output.
limits: Methods differ, so Fisler says direct comparison is imprecise. Ebrahimi's students had learned imperative LISP. The Simon table layout in the PDF text is partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Famous low success rates on Rainfall depend on instruction. Do not treat 'composition is hard' as a fixed fact about plans.

source: Fisler (2014) The recurring rainfall problem (ICER 2014)
finding: A Java CS1 instructor ran the same problem with arrays and no lists. Nearly all used one loop.
numbers: N = 51: 50 Single Loop (28 for, 12 while, 8 a while nested in a for); 1 student used two loops in sequence; 2 used a second array.
limits: One instructor; not coded for low-level errors.
agent_relevance: The available data structure sets the available plans. Give the agent the structure that makes the clean plan easy.

source: Fisler and Castro (2017) Sometimes, Rainfall accumulates: talk-alouds with novice functional programmers (ICER 2017)
finding: A talk-aloud study of how novices choose and switch between several schemas that all fit one problem. A few students still struggle where most do well. The paper describes what makes them pick, change or drop a schema, and when they notice it is failing.
numbers: Four students in narrative case studies. Context: in the earlier 218-student sample, 186 had a mostly correct solution.
limits: Qualitative, N=4, end of a CS1 course. Cannot give rates.
agent_relevance: Schema switching is a real event with its own triggers. A switch should be allowed, and driven by a failing check, as in our guardrails.

source: Fisler and Castro (2017) Sometimes, Rainfall accumulates: talk-alouds with novice functional programmers (ICER 2017)
finding: Review of plan models: Spohrer and Soloway say novices refine a stored plan; Pirolli found novices adapt solutions they already know; Rist says retrieval (top-down) when a schema exists, creation (bottom-up from a focus) when not. None cover choosing among several partly known schemas.
numbers: Earlier Adding Machine study (Castro and Fisler): students followed the design recipe into a structure that did not suit the problem and did quite poorly.
limits: Summary of other work as cited by these authors.
agent_relevance: A schema library needs a selection step. Retrieval is not enough when two stored plans both match.

source: Castro and Fisler (2020) Qualitative analyses of movements between task-level and code-level thinking of novice programmers (SIGCSE 2020)
finding: Students who moved back and forth between naming tasks and writing code (a cyclic pattern) tended to produce near-correct solutions. Students who only named tasks, or only wrote code, did not.
numbers: 22 think-aloud participants (12 in course 1, 10 in course 2) on Rainfall and Max-Temps. In Rainfall at least half of each cohort were cyclic and generally close to correct. None of the code-focused or one-way students produced correct solutions.
limits: Small, qualitative, chosen from larger sign-up pools. Closeness to correct was judged by the authors.
agent_relevance: Make the agent state task roles and how tasks connect, then write code, then return to the tasks. A plan with no links between tasks is not enough.

source: Castro and Fisler (2020) Qualitative analyses of movements between task-level and code-level thinking of novice programmers (SIGCSE 2020)
finding: Retrieved patterns failed in recognisable ways. Students missed that the -999 sentinel plays the same role as the empty list. They put the average formula inside the recursive case because the list template was retrieved mechanically. They did not see the limits of the pattern they retrieved.
numbers: Rainfall: sentinel handling was where students got stuck. One student wrote the average formula inside the template's recursive case.
limits: Four observations from think-aloud transcripts; no counts per observation.
agent_relevance: The main schema failure is over-application: a stored plan fires on surface cues and is not checked against the problem. Add a check that each stored plan's assumptions hold.

source: Castro and Fisler (2020) Qualitative analyses of movements between task-level and code-level thinking of novice programmers (SIGCSE 2020)
finding: When stuck, students stayed stuck. They did not go back to the design-recipe steps they had been taught, even when those steps would have helped.
numbers: Reported across both courses; no rate given.
limits: Qualitative.
agent_relevance: An instruction to 'review the method' is not used when the agent is stuck. A program should trigger the fallback step on a signal.

source: Rivera, Steinmaurer, Fisler, Krishnamurthi (2024) Iterative student program planning using transformer-driven feedback (ITiCSE 2024)
finding: An LLM turned students' written plans into code, and hand-written tests were run on that code, so students got feedback on their plan. GPT-3.5, InstructGPT and StarCoder gave too many false negatives (adequate plans, failing code), so GPT-4 was used. False positives were rare and false negatives moderate.
numbers: 544 of 736 enrolled students submitted. False positives: 13 plans coded wrong, 12 of them scored 0/5 or 1/5. False negatives: first attempt 39 right-track plans, 27 failed most tests; last attempt 42 right-track, 19 failed.
limits: Plan quality hand-coded for only a sample of 50 students. The prompt told the LLM to translate step by step and not fix errors; results depend on that.
agent_relevance: A plan can be graded by running code built from it. Use tests as the verdict on a plan, not a model's opinion of it. Expect false negatives from the translator.

source: Rivera, Steinmaurer, Fisler, Krishnamurthi (2024) Iterative student program planning using transformer-driven feedback (ITiCSE 2024)
finding: Week-3 CS1 students wrote real plans, not copies of the problem, for problems they could not yet program, and revised after feedback. Novices wrote mostly prose, and only about a third used the suggested labelled-steps layout.
numbers: Sample of 50 students: 10 experienced, 10 novice, 30 unknown. Prose was about 70% of novice plans. Extraneous detail: about 25% of novices. Very few plans just restated the problem.
limits: Groups defined by what students volunteered, not tested. 50 of 544 analysed.
agent_relevance: Natural-language plans can be good enough to guide code. Do not require a fixed plan format.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Self-planning code generation with large language models (ACM TOSEM)
finding: Asking the model for a short numbered plan first, then writing code from it, beat direct generation and beat chain-of-thought code generation. A reference plan did much better still.
numbers: code-davinci-002, HumanEval Pass@1: direct 48.1, few-shot 52.6, code CoT 53.9 (+12.1% relative), self-planning 60.3 (+25.4%), ground-truth plan 74.4 (+54.7%). MBPP-sanitized Pass@1: direct 49.8, CoT 54.5, self-planning 55.7 (+11.8%), ground-truth plan 65.1 (+30.7%).
limits: One older base model family. Plan prompts are few-shot, hand-written. Ground-truth plans were produced with the authors' own few-shot pipeline and validated, so 74.4 is not a clean human number.
agent_relevance: A plan step gives a real gain but the plan the agent writes recovers only part of what a good plan gives (60.3 vs 74.4). Plan quality is the limit.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Self-planning code generation with large language models (ACM TOSEM)
finding: Planning helps only when the model is big enough, and detailed solution steps cut diversity. Self-planning kept diversity as sample count rose, while chain-of-thought lost it.
numbers: HumanEval Pass@k at k = 1/2/5/10: direct 48.1/55.1/64.7/75.0; code CoT 53.9/56.4/63.5/68.6; self-planning 60.3/66.0/70.5/76.3; ground-truth plan 74.4/75.6/85.3/89.1. Small models (4-shot): text-curie-001 6.7B direct 34.0, self-planning 30.1, with the large model's plan 44.9; code-cushman-001 13B direct 48.1, self-planning 50.0, with the large model's plan 57.1.
limits: 164 HumanEval problems. Small-model rows use a different shot setting and the table labels are shifted in the PDF text.
agent_relevance: A weak model that writes its own plan may lose; a stronger model's plan helps it. Do not make plans so detailed that all samples copy them.

source: Li, Li, Li, Jin (2023) Structured chain-of-thought prompting for code generation (arXiv 2305.06599)
finding: Reasoning steps written in the three program structures (sequence, branch, loop) beat free-text chain-of-thought for code. Plain CoT helped little.
numbers: ChatGPT HumanEval Pass@1: zero-shot 49.73, few-shot 52.47, CoT 53.29, structured CoT 60.64 (+13.79% over CoT). MBPP +12.31% and MBCPP +6.63% over CoT. CoT over few-shot: up to 2% on HumanEval, 7.51% on MBPP, 3.79% on MBCPP.
limits: Gains shrink at Pass@5 (2.38% on HumanEval). Same OpenAI model family. A review by 10 developers preferred structured-CoT programs.
agent_relevance: Plans with the shape of code (steps, branches, loops) help more than prose plans. Our plan templates should be structured, not free text.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Planning in natural language improves LLM search for code generation (arXiv 2409.03733)
finding: A correct idea sketch is nearly sufficient for a correct program, and idea quality is almost all-or-nothing. This is the reason to search over plans instead of code.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini on LiveCodeBench: a back-translated solution sketch as short as 10 tokens raised accuracy significantly. With 5 self-generated ideas per problem and 25 samples each (75 problems, 375 sketches, problems at 0% and 100% removed), solve rates polarised to near 0% or near 100% per sketch.
limits: One model for this experiment. The generated-idea part is correlational.
agent_relevance: The plan is the unit that decides success. Spend sampling budget on different plans, checked by running, not on more code from the same plan.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Planning in natural language improves LLM search for code generation (arXiv 2409.03733)
finding: Searching over many plans (observations first, then plans built from them) beat repeated sampling of code. It lowered pass@1 for some models but raised pass@200.
numbers: Pass@1 / pass@200 / IdeaSearch@200 / PlanSearch@200 on LiveCodeBench: GPT-4o-mini 39.0/53.3/59.4/64.9; GPT-4o 41.3/60.6/70.4/73.0; DeepSeek-Coder-V2 41.4/53.2/65.9/70.3; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 40.3/55.6/70.2/77.0. With public-test filtering, PlanSearch reached 77.1% after 20 submissions.
limits: PlanSearch often lowers pass@1 (the authors say so). The diversity score is LLM-judged, and explains much of the variance in relative gain.
agent_relevance: Plan diversity is the lever when samples from one model are alike (our G4). Use tests to pick among plans, and expect no gain at pass@1.

source: Ridnik, Kredo, Friedman (2024) Code generation with AlphaCodium: from prompt engineering to flow engineering (arXiv 2401.08500)
finding: A fixed multi-stage flow (problem reflection, solution possibilities, ranked choice, AI-written tests, repair with test anchors) beat one well-designed direct prompt on CodeContests.
numbers: GPT-4 pass@5 on the validation set: 19% with a direct prompt, 44% with the flow. Test anchors guard against repairs that break tests already passed.
limits: Whole-flow comparison; per-stage effect sizes not taken here. CodeContests only. AI-written tests can be wrong, which is why anchors exist.
agent_relevance: Staged plans with test-based repair and tests as a guard are well supported. The gain comes from the program controlling the flow.

source: Le et al. (2024) CodeChain: towards modular code generation through chain of self-revisions with representative sub-modules (ICLR 2024)
finding: Asking for modular code, then clustering the sub-modules across samples and feeding representative ones back for revision, raised pass rates. Modular prompting alone, without the revision loop, hurt.
numbers: Relative pass@1 gain of 35% on APPS and 76% on CodeContests. APPS validation, 20-problem subset: CodeChain+GPT4 61.50 vs Self-repair+GPT4 with human feedback 52.60 and with GPT4 feedback 33.30.
limits: Pass@1 on APPS subsets; the 20-sample comparison is tiny. The ablation table is garbled in the PDF text, so only headline numbers are used. Clustering alone was not enough; filtering by public tests first was needed.
agent_relevance: A library of solved sub-modules, chosen as cluster centres of tested samples, works as stored plans. Modularity by prompting alone can hurt; the reuse step is what pays.

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions (ICML 2024)
finding: Refactoring solved programs into a library of helper functions, verified by running, improved a weaker model's accuracy when the library was retrieved at test time.
numbers: CodeLlama-13B absolute accuracy gains: +11.5 on LOGO, +26.1 on Date, +8.1 on TextCraft; with REGAL it beat GPT-3.5 without abstractions by 19.2 on LOGO. Ablations (dev, CodeLlama-13B; full 55.0 LOGO, 77.0 Date, 34.12 TextCraft): no retry 48.3/51.9/30.43; no curriculum 36.3/56.6/28.78; no code-bank pruning 52.0/65.5/25.26; no code-bank editing 53.3/69.6/27.35.
limits: About 200 training examples. Gains small or unclear in math domains with no clear domain language (MATH, TabMWP); Lemur-70B gave many empty outputs there.
agent_relevance: Stored subroutines help when verified by running and learned from easy to hard. Order mattered a lot (random order: 18.7 points lower on LOGO).

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions (ICML 2024)
finding: Boundary: the benefit of a plan library shrinks as the base model gets stronger.
numbers: Date with GPT-3.5-turbo: primitive-only 88.9 vs REGAL 90.2 (+1.3), against CodeLlama-13B 45.6 vs 57.1 (+11.5). TextCraft: CodeLlama-34B 22.2 vs 30.8.
limits: Single run per cell in what was read; no error bars in the quoted text.
agent_relevance: Our agent is strong, so expect a small gain from a plan library on tasks it already solves, and more on rare or domain-specific plans.

source: Zelikman, Huang, Poesia, Goodman, Haber (2023) Parsel: algorithmic reasoning with language models by composing decompositions (arXiv 2212.10561)
finding: Decompose a task into function descriptions, implement each function several ways, and test combinations. The plan alone was not the cause of the gain; the composition and testing step was.
numbers: APPS competition-level pass rate rose from 14.5% to 25.5% with Parsel. Ablation: the same high-level plans translated straight to Python at the same budget (16 implementations per plan, 100 problems) gave 6% vs 25.5% and solved a strict subset. HumanEval pass@1 with GPT-4: 67% to 85%.
limits: Codex-era model; ablation on 100 sampled problems. Generated tests used for HumanEval pass@1 can be wrong.
agent_relevance: A plan helps most when its parts can be checked and recombined by code. A plan written in words and then coded in one shot gave 6%.

source: Soloway and Ehrlich (1984) Empirical studies of programming knowledge (IEEE Trans. Software Eng. SE-10(5))
finding: Founding study of programming plans and rules of discourse. Plan-like programs, which follow stereotyped plans and discourse rules, are easier for experts to understand and recall than unplan-like programs that break the rules.
numbers: Not read this session; numbers not recorded. A secondary page says the study used fill-in-the-blank and recall tests with novice, intermediate and expert programmers.
limits: Not opened; the summary comes from search snippets and citing papers. A later experimental paper argued plans alone do not explain novice-expert differences and that selection and discourse rules matter, with plan structure dominating at intermediate skill. Check numbers before use.
agent_relevance: Plan knowledge is a retrieval aid; code that breaks expectations is harder to follow, plausibly for a model as well as a person.

source: Gilmore and Green (1988) Programming plans and programming expertise (Quarterly J. Exp. Psychology 40A); also Gilmore (1987) Are programming plans psychologically real outside Pascal?
finding: A challenge to plan theory: the expert advantage on plan-like code may depend on the notation, so plans may be partly a product of the language and its layout, not a fixed mental structure.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Only titles seen in a bibliographic search. The direction of the result is from memory of the literature and unverified.
agent_relevance: If plan structure is partly notation-driven, a plan library should be tied to the form in which the agent reads code.

source: Ebrahimi (1994) Novice programmer errors: language constructs and plan composition (Int. J. Human-Computer Studies 41)
finding: Studied Rainfall in four languages (C, FORTRAN, Pascal, LISP) with an error taxonomy. Its codes became the base for later Rainfall coding.
numbers: Only through Fisler (2014): the 20 LISP students had missing if-guards 50%, misplaced updates 40%, malformed updates 40%, spurious output 40%.
limits: Not opened; figures second-hand. LISP students had learned imperative LISP.
agent_relevance: Guards for edge cases (divide by zero, empty input) are the most commonly omitted piece. Check for them by running.

source: Simon (2013) Soloway's rainfall problem has become harder (LaTiCE 2013)
finding: A Rainfall replication in a C# CS1 with the input given in a data structure; students still did poorly.
numbers: Only through Fisler (2014): 149 students; 36% no pertinent code, 22% loop ended by sentinel, 21% counted days in loop, 40% ignored negatives, 0% guarded the division.
limits: Not opened; row labels read from a table with damaged layout, so the match of figures to rows is uncertain.
agent_relevance: Plan composition failure rates remain high in a standard imperative course, even without I/O.

source: Spohrer, Soloway, Pope (1985) A goal/plan analysis of buggy Pascal programs; Spohrer and Soloway (1986)
finding: Goal and plan analysis of student bugs. Per Castro and Fisler, most novice mistakes come from plan composition, not language constructs.
numbers: Only through Castro and Fisler (2020): 'most of novice programmers' mistakes come from plan composition'. No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened; the claim is as cited. Fisler (2014) found few composition errors in a functional-first course, so this is not universal.
agent_relevance: Bug classes in model-written code may also trace to missing plans and interleaved tasks; log which plan each failure belongs to.

source: Rist (1989; 1991) plan retrieval and plan creation models
finding: Programmers follow plan retrieval (top-down, when a schema exists) or plan creation (bottom-up from a focus line, when it does not). Experts shift toward retrieval but fall back to creation on hard problems.
numbers: Only through Scholtz and Wiedenbeck (1992): strong plan creation in novices, shifting to retrieval with experience; even experienced programmers used creation on difficult problems.
limits: Not opened; second-hand. Exact titles not verified.
agent_relevance: Offer a stored plan if the schema matches; otherwise build from the core computation. Difficulty should push the agent toward building, not recalling.

source: de Raadt et al. on explicit teaching of planning strategies, using Rainfall (as cited in Fisler and Castro 2017)
finding: Rainfall was used to test explicit teaching of planning strategies.
numbers: Only that it exists: Fisler and Castro say the paper does not discuss changes in strategy. No effect sizes recorded.
limits: Not opened; year and title not verified (year set to 0 for unknown). The link points to the citing paper.
agent_relevance: Open question: whether explicit plan instruction changes plan choice. Test ours with an A/B on plan hints.

source: Ginat, Menashe, Taya (2013) Novice difficulties with interleaved pattern composition (ISSEP 2013), as cited in Fisler 2014
finding: Novices have trouble interleaving algorithmic patterns into one loop. Fisler disagrees with the authors' preference for interleaved solutions in CS1.
numbers: Cited only; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. The link points to the citing paper.
agent_relevance: Interleaving is the hard step. Where possible keep pieces separate and combine them by code.
